title: Executive Interview with James Huang of AlChip - Semiwiki
gist: An interview with James Huang, Director of Engineering at Alchip Technologies, arguing that TSMC CoWoS advanced packaging has crossed from an optimization for a few high-end parts into an architectural requirement for mainstream AI and HPC silicon — because compute performance no longer scales on its own. Huang's core thesis is that CoWoS-S, CoWoS-R and CoWoS-L will coexist rather than converge, that packaging must be co-designed with silicon from the architecture phase, and that supply-chain execution (packaging capacity, HBM availability, ramp) is now as decisive as design skill.

themes.theme: Advanced packaging crosses into architectural necessity

insights.claim: Advanced packaging has shifted from an optimization applied to a limited number of high-end applications into an architectural requirement for many AI and HPC designs, according to Alchip's Director of Engineering James Huang.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: If packaging is now mandatory rather than optional, CoWoS capacity becomes a gating input on AI silicon supply, not a discretionary upgrade.
insights.quote: A few years ago, advanced packaging was viewed as an optimization for a limited number of high-end applications. Today, it has become an architectural requirement for many AI and HPC designs.
insights.locator: AI has fundamentally changed the design priorities

insights.claim: The stated root cause of the packaging shift is that compute performance is no longer scaling fast enough on its own, forcing integration of multiple compute chiplets with HBM and high-speed I/O within practical power, yield and manufacturability limits.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The end of straightforward compute scaling is the structural driver of the packaging cycle — it will not reverse with a node transition.
insights.quote: compute performance is no longer scaling fast enough on its own
insights.locator: The primary reason is that compute performance

insights.claim: More companies including hyperscalers and AI startups are developing custom silicon because they want differentiated architectures rather than off-the-shelf solutions, with advanced packaging identified as a key enabler of that differentiation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Custom ASIC demand is broadening beyond the top hyperscalers — the addressable customer set for design-service providers is widening.
insights.locator: Another important trend is that more companies

insights.claim: CoWoS-S uses a silicon interposer, delivers the highest interconnect density, and is optimized for bandwidth-intensive applications such as AI training accelerators with multiple HBM stacks.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: CoWoS-S is the variant tied to the highest-value training silicon — its capacity is the tightest constraint in the AI supply chain.
insights.locator: CoWoS-S is based on a silicon interposer

insights.claim: CoWoS-R uses redistribution layers and provides greater flexibility and cost advantages for designs that do not require ultra-high routing density.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: CoWoS-R is the cost-down escape valve for inference and networking parts — a relief path when interposer capacity is scarce.
insights.locator: CoWoS-R uses redistribution layers

insights.claim: CoWoS-S and CoWoS-R are complementary rather than competing options, with the choice set by device architecture, bandwidth requirements, package size and cost objectives.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A four-variable selection rule for reading which packaging line any new accelerator will consume.
insights.quote: Rather than viewing them as competing technologies, we see them as complementary options.
insights.locator: These technologies address different optimization points

insights.claim: Alchip has participated in multiple advanced-node ASIC programs using both CoWoS-S and CoWoS-R across AI, HPC and networking applications over the past several years, building experience in silicon-package co-design, HBM integration, power integrity and thermal optimization.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Establishes Alchip as a credible second-source design-service partner for CoWoS AI ASICs beyond the market leaders.
insights.locator: Over the past several years, Alchip has participated

themes.theme: Packaging as system architecture, not back-end step

insights.claim: CoWoS should not be treated as a packaging technology added at the end of a project; packaging decisions drive die partitioning, floor planning, memory architecture, power delivery, thermal management and verification.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Packaging choice locks in downstream design cost — it is decided far earlier in the customer's cycle than most supply-chain models assume.
insights.quote: We don’t see CoWoS as a packaging technology that is added at the end of a project. We see it as an integral part of the system architecture.
insights.locator: We don’t see CoWoS as a packaging technology

insights.claim: Successful CoWoS programs require silicon and package co-design from the earliest planning stages, with foundry, packaging, IP and EDA partners engaged holistically rather than sequentially.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Multi-partner orchestration capability is the real moat for ASIC service providers — hard to replicate and sticky once established.
insights.locator: That is why successful CoWoS programs require silicon and package co-design

insights.claim: Architectural decisions made early in a project — chiplet partitioning strategy, HBM organization, die size optimization, power budgeting and package selection — have a disproportionate impact on program success, yield, manufacturability, verification complexity and time-to-market.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Front-loaded architecture effort is the cheapest lever on AI ASIC schedule risk — a checklist for diligencing any custom silicon program.
insights.quote: architectural decisions made early in the project have a disproportionate impact on overall program success
insights.locator: One of the most important lessons we have learned

insights.claim: There is no single optimal chiplet partitioning strategy; customers must balance bandwidth versus latency, die size versus yield, process-node optimization, power efficiency and package complexity.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The absence of a dominant partitioning recipe means design-service expertise stays scarce and commands pricing power.
insights.quote: There is no single optimal partitioning strategy.
insights.locator: There is no single optimal partitioning strategy

themes.theme: Power and thermal as system-level problems

insights.claim: Power delivery in large multi-chip packages is becoming a system-level challenge rather than only a chip-level one, requiring coordinated silicon, package and board design to hold IR drop and signal integrity.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Power-delivery IP and board-level co-design gain importance in the AI BOM — a widening niche for PMIC and substrate specialists.
insights.quote: One trend we see clearly is that power delivery is becoming a system-level challenge, rather than only a chip-level challenge.
insights.locator: Power density continues to increase rapidly

insights.claim: Thermal analysis for advanced AI ASICs must begin during architectural planning because chiplet placement, HBM arrangement, power distribution and package selection all determine the cooling strategy — and waiting until physical implementation often forces costly redesigns.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Cooling requirements are locked at architecture time, meaning data center thermal design is effectively decided years before deployment.
insights.quote: Waiting until physical implementation to address thermal issues often leads to costly redesigns.
insights.locator: Thermal considerations should be addressed much earlier

insights.claim: Power density continues to increase rapidly, particularly in AI accelerators, making it a named and worsening constraint rather than a solved engineering problem.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Rising power density per package sustains structural demand for liquid cooling and advanced power delivery through the next generations.
insights.locator: Power density continues to increase rapidly

insights.claim: Verification in CoWoS heterogeneous multi-die systems must extend beyond silicon functionality to cover die-to-die interfaces, package behavior, power delivery, thermal conditions and system-level operating requirements.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Expanding verification scope is a direct tailwind for multi-physics EDA and system-level verification tool vendors.
insights.locator: Verification complexity increases significantly

insights.claim: The industry is moving toward integrated verification methodologies that evaluate silicon and package behavior together rather than independently.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Watch for EDA consolidation and tool acquisitions bridging chip and package domains — that is where the methodology gap sits.
insights.locator: Verification complexity increases significantly

insights.claim: Critical CoWoS program risks named are packaging capacity, HBM availability, manufacturing yield, test strategy, production scheduling and ramp execution — requiring coordination across foundry, packaging, memory, test and assembly partners.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A concrete risk register for AI ASIC programs — packaging capacity and HBM availability head the list, both externally constrained.
insights.locator: CoWoS programs require close coordination

insights.claim: Successful CoWoS execution depends not only on technical excellence but on disciplined program management across the entire supply chain, which is where experienced ASIC service providers claim to add value.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Program management, not IP, is the pitched differentiator for design-service firms — a services margin story rather than a licensing one.
insights.locator: CoWoS programs require close coordination

insights.claim: CoWoS-L is expected to support new classes of AI and HPC systems requiring higher scalability than current packaging technologies can efficiently provide, as customers need larger packages, higher interconnect density and more flexible chiplet integration.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: CoWoS-L is the next capacity bottleneck to monitor as AI package sizes scale past what -S and -R support.
insights.locator: CoWoS-L represents another important step

insights.claim: CoWoS-S, CoWoS-R and CoWoS-L are expected to coexist rather than converge, with designers selecting among them based on architecture, bandwidth, package size, power objectives, manufacturability, schedule and cost targets.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Contradicts the assumption of a single winning packaging standard — TSMC's packaging capacity mix stays fragmented and harder to forecast.
insights.quote: As these requirements increase, designers are unlikely to converge on a single packaging technology.
insights.locator: We expect CoWoS-S, CoWoS-R, and CoWoS-L to coexist

insights.claim: Future AI ASICs will require more chiplets, higher HBM bandwidth and capacity, heterogeneous process technologies, more sophisticated power delivery and stronger silicon-package co-optimization.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous process mixing means mature-node capacity gets pulled into AI packages too — not just leading-edge demand.
insights.locator: We expect CoWoS-S, CoWoS-R, and CoWoS-L to coexist

insights.claim: Alchip explicitly positions itself as technology-neutral across CoWoS variants, aiming to help designers pick the best balance of performance, manufacturability, schedule and total system cost rather than promoting one option.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Neutrality is the design-service business model — value accrues from advising across options, not owning a technology.
insights.quote: the goal is not to promote one packaging technology over another
insights.locator: From Alchip’s perspective, the goal is not to promote
